issues.title: [Bug]  client-controlled values closing the session with no error event
issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version.
- [x] 3. Please note that if the bug-related issue you submitted lacks corresponding environment info and a minimal reproducible demo, it will be challenging for us to reproduce and resolve the issue, reducing the likelihood of receiving feedback.
- [x] 4. If the issue you raised is not a bug but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 5. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`RealtimeSession` rejects three client-controlled values with a bare `assert`
(`sglang_omni/serve/realtime/session.py`):

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/627e74b8c01bfce3e2cec4d1b0a39adc695f68e8/sglang_omni/serve/realtime/session.py#L160-L161 

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/627e74b8c01bfce3e2cec4d1b0a39adc695f68e8/sglang_omni/serve/realtime/session.py#L165-L166

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/627e74b8c01bfce3e2cec4d1b0a39adc695f68e8/sglang_omni/serve/realtime/session.py#L197

None of these is a server-side invariant. Each is a value the WebSocket client picks: the shape of
the frame, the `type` field, and a `session.update` parameter.

**What happens.** Neither `run()` nor `dispatch()` catches anything, and the endpoint wraps the
session in `try/finally` with no `except` (`sglang_omni/serve/openai_api.py`, `_register_realtime`):

```python
await websocket.accept()
session = manager.open(websocket)
try:
    await session.run()
finally:
    await manager.close(session.session_id)
```

So an `AssertionError` reaches the ASGI layer, which closes the connection. The client gets no
`error` event explaining what it did wrong, and the session loses any buffered audio. A typo in
`type`, or one stray non-object frame, ends the session instead of being reported.

The third case needs nothing unusual from the client, because the session schema advertises the
values that trip it (`sglang_omni/serve/realtime/events.py`):

```python
input_audio_format: Literal["pcm16", "g711_ulaw", "g711_alaw"] | None = None
```

A client that reads the schema and sends `g711_ulaw` gets its socket closed with no explanation.

**The same message already rejects the sibling field properly.** This file uses `send_error` for
`unsupported_modality`, `invalid_content_index`, `item_not_found`, and, on the line immediately
below the third assert, for the output audio format:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/627e74b8c01bfce3e2cec4d1b0a39adc695f68e8/sglang_omni/serve/realtime/session.py#L198-L204

One `session.update` message, two different contracts for the same class of mistake.

**A second, latent failure mode.** `python -O` strips the asserts. Two of the three then fall through
into a more confusing downstream exception, and the third silently succeeds:

| value | default interpreter | `python -O` |
|---|---|---|
| non-object frame | `AssertionError` | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` in `parse_client_event` |
| unrecognized `type` | `AssertionError` | `KeyError: <class 'NoneType'>` on the `HANDLERS` lookup |
| `input_audio_format: g711_ulaw` | `AssertionError` | **`session.updated` granting `g711_ulaw`** |

Nothing in this repository runs `python -O` today, so this mode is latent rather than an active
production bug. The last row is t

issues.title: [Comm] Record the failure paths, and run a soak when the comm layer changes
issues.body:
## English

### Summary

This issue asks for two things.

**First, trace events on the paths that fail.** The comm data plane emits eight events today. All eight record success. The layer emits nothing when a transfer fails. It emits nothing when it keeps slots after a failure. It emits nothing when it keeps a pending entry after a failure. If any of these happen in production, the logs show nothing.

We scoped this to four events on the slot-pool path when we opened the issue. Since then we read the paged KV path and found a larger gap, described below. #1595 implements the KV part.

**Second, a soak that runs only when the comm layer changes.** We ran one for 8 hours and it answered a question that no unit test answers: does the layer leak resources under sustained load? A soak costs a GPU for hours, so it must not run on every pull request. It should run when a pull request touches `sglang_omni/comm/` or `sglang_omni/relay/`.

The two parts connect. The soak reads the trace events. Without events on the failure paths, a soak can only report that nothing crashed.

Neither part changes behaviour. Neither part asks you to choose a recovery policy.

### The paged KV path has no events at all

The eight events all sit on the slot-pool path. Paged KV transfer uses pre-registered pools and page indices instead of slots, so none of them fire for it. We checked every function: thirteen functions across `comm/engine.py` and `relay/cuda_ipc.py`, about 500 lines, contain no `_comm_trace` call. `send_kv_pages` is 113 lines, `get_kv_pages` is 108, `prepare_kv_receive` is 58, and none of them record anything.

`get_kv_pages` also constructs its operation with `emit_trace=False`, so the one place where an existing event could have fired is switched off.

Prefill/decode disaggregation will run its traffic over this path. Today that traffic would produce no log line, on success or on failure.

Two smaller gaps sit next to it.

**The router never records which transport an edge selected.** An edge that falls back keeps working, so every counter still reads as healthy. We lost an eight-hour soak to this: one edge moved from `cuda_ipc` to `shm` after the first request, the run reported balanced ACK counts and flat memory, and the path under test carried no traffic. Nothing in the log said so.

**The direct-IPC stream path records only its sender.** `send_stream_chunk` and `_run_stream_send` emit; `outbound_stream` and `read_stream_chunk` do not. That path has no byte ceiling, and measuring the held bytes needs both rates, so the missing consumer event makes the growth unmeasurable.

#1595 adds fourteen events for these three gaps and keeps them behind the same environment variable. The four events in Part 1 below still apply to the slot-pool path and are not covered by that pull request.

### Why to add the events now

Two pieces of work will soon need data that the layer cannot produce today.

**Paged KV transfer.** #1315 and #1382 are merged. No pipeline code calls them yet. When some code does call them, the plane will carry a second kind of allocation. Those allocations use pages, not slots. They are much larger than today's per-token traffic. If you add the events first, the first integration starts with a baseline.

**Cross-node relay.** #862 Phase 3 states that the data plane must prove itself before the orchestration layer depends on it. A proof needs the same measurements on every transport. The eight events already have the right shape. They on

issues.title: [MOSS TTS Realtime] Preserve codec decoder state across turns
issues.body:
talk110 is one continuous ACL6060 benchmark talk, not 194 independent conversations. InfiniSST translated it online and emitted 194 Chinese text chunks. We sent each chunk to MOSS-TTS-Realtime as one TTS turn so its audio could be played immediately. All 194 turns belong to the same logical speaker session. The boundary under test is therefore an application-level streaming turn boundary, not a session boundary.

PR #1410 preserves the acoustic model history across successful turns, but the vocoder state still ends at each turn. It keeps one process-wide codec.streaming context, then leases one codec slot to each request. When a turn finishes, decode_delta drains the pending frames and releases the slot. _CodecStreamSession.release resets that slot, so the next turn in the same session starts with fresh causal codec state.

We verified the effect with this 194 turn talk. The audio codes were generated once, then the same 8,581 frames were decoded in two ways. Resetting the decoder at every turn caused clear speaker changes. Keeping one decoder context for the full talk was noticeably more consistent in human A/B. Both outputs were 686.48 seconds and 16,475,520 samples.

Turn completion should emit all pending PCM without resetting the session-owned codec slot. The slot should be released on session close, TTL expiry, abort, or failure. Different sessions must remain isolated.

A regression test can run two turns with one session_id and verify that codec state continues across the boundary. A new session or a closed session should start fresh. The fixed-code service output can also be compared with one continuous codec decode.

Reproduction and report:

https://github.com/luojiaxuan/S2S_omni/blob/a2eb237/docs/moss_realtime_codec_context_issue.md

https://github.com/luojiaxuan/S2S_omni/blob/a2eb237/scripts/codec_decoder_context_ab.py

https://github.com/luojiaxuan/S2S_omni/blob/a2eb237/projects/infinisst_moss_tts_cascade/artifacts/codec_decoder_context_ab_talk110/report.json

This applies to #1410. It is separate from #801, which tracks codec state correctness and CUDA graphs inside one streaming request.

issues.title: [Tracking][Pipeline] Process-level replicas
issues.body:
## Summary

This issue tracks the implementation and productionization of process-level replicas in the SGLang-Omni pipeline runtime.

## Motivation

Replicating the entire pipeline applies the same data-parallel configuration to every process, even when only one part of the pipeline is saturated. This can duplicate unnecessary model state and leave CPU cores or GPUs underutilized. Process-level replicas provide finer-grained data parallelism by allowing each process group to scale independently according to its workload and available resources.

## Existing work

- #1131 defines the original runtime-level stage-replica design and the Qwen3-Omni performance target.
- #1175 implements stage-level replica expansion, request-sticky round-robin binding, binding propagation, logical target resolution, and the initial Qwen3-Omni deployment.
- #1262 is a draft follow-up for replicated entry stages and logical source normalization at fan-in and streaming boundaries.
- #1276 record Higgs TTS replica benchmark results and documentation.

## TODO

1. **Replace stage-level replicas with process-level replicas.**  
   Replicate a complete process group instead of expanding each stage independently. Stages and TP ranks within the same process should share one replica identity and request binding while preserving local state and process topology.

2. **Support replicated entry stages.**  
   Allow the entry stage to belong to a replicated process group. The Coordinator should select a concrete entry replica during admission and verify that all configured entry replicas are ready before serving requests.

3. **Support fan-in from replicated stages.**  
   Model-facing fan-in APIs should continue using logical stage names even when data comes from a physical replica such as `encoder@r1`. Transport routing, ACKs, ordering, and observability should retain the physical replica identity.

4. **Validate compatibility across model pipelines.**  
   Test process-level replicas across representative TTS, multimodal, and TP-enabled pipelines, covering startup, inference, streaming, abort, output parity, and performance. Track each discovered incompatibility in a child issue and fix runtime-generic problems in the framework.

5. **Add request-hash cache-affinity routing.**  
   Add a deterministic routing policy that sends requests sharing reusable context to the same replica, using a stable session or prefix/cache key rather than only a unique request ID. Compare its cache-hit rate, latency, throughput, and load balance against round-robin routing.

6. **Add metrics and tooling for automated performance tuning.**  
   Expose machine-readable per-process and per-replica metrics such as queue depth, in-flight requests, service time, batch size, throughput, tail latency, cache-hit rate, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory pressure. Provide profiling, benchmarking, and configuration-search tools so future autotuners can optimize replica counts, placement, routing policies, and runtime parameters for the best workload-specific performance.

issues.title: [Perf] Extend MOSS-TTS Delay sampling CUDA Graph to feedback embedding
issues.body:
PR: #1792 
## Motivation

MOSS-TTS Delay still leaves one repeat-per-decode-step operation eager after the existing sampling CUDA Graph in #1303: feedback embedding for the sampled 33-channel row.

This is a direct follow-up to the MOSS-TTS optimization tracker #1233, under the **AR sampling** workstream. The earlier profiling investigation #1232 identified launch-heavy eager sampling/feedback work outside the backbone CUDA Graph as the dominant AR-side optimization direction; #1303 captured sampling and Delay-FSM updates, but feedback embedding intentionally remained eager.

Current decode flow is effectively:

```text
backbone decode CUDA Graph
  -> eager LM heads
  -> sampling CUDA Graph (#1303)
  -> eager feedback embedding
  -> next decode step
```

The feedback embedding path performs 33 embedding lookups plus sequential accumulation through `_prepare_multi_modal_inputs(rows)` on every decode step.

## Qualification results

A self-contained timing probe on H200 measured feedback embedding at roughly **1.5-2.0 ms per decode step**, about one third of the measured `decode_collect` GPU time in the sampled c8/c16 runs. The cost scaled weakly with batch size, consistent with a launch/latency-heavy path rather than a throughput-efficient batched kernel.

A diagnostic CUDA Graph that captured only feedback embedding passed exact `torch.equal` checks for the captured batch buckets. This diagnostic is not the proposed production design.

For service-level validation, the benchmark methodology was first calibrated with a true A/A null control. The final protocol uses two exclusive H200s simultaneously, explicit CPU-core partitioning, warm reference caches, and physical-GPU crossover so fixed GPU-speed differences cancel.

Null control, c16, 192 warmup + 192 measured samples, 4 rounds:

| Metric | Crossover effect |
| --- | ---: |
| QPS | -0.41% |
| Audio throughput | -0.41% |
| Mean latency | -0.50% |
| Mean RTF | -0.51% |
| ITL | +0.19% |

The null also exposed an approximately 2.5 percentage-point physical-GPU difference, which the crossover estimator cancels.

Diagnostic feedback-graph A/B, same protocol, 8 rounds:

| Metric | Crossover effect | Placement consistency |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| QPS | **+1.29%** | +0.71% / +1.87% |
| Audio throughput | **+1.30%** | +0.70% / +1.90% |
| Mean latency | **+1.24%** | +0.67% / +1.81% |
| Mean RTF | **+1.24%** | +0.65% / +1.83% |
| TTFC | +0.20% | near flat, as expected |
| ITL | **+7.99%** | +7.34% / +8.64%, 8/8 wins |

Mean generated audio duration was identical between arms in both the null and candidate runs.

The strongest evidence is the ITL result: the optimization targets repeated decode-step feedback work, and the improvement is large, consistent across both physical GPU placements, and absent from the null control. The smaller end-to-end QPS/latency gain is directionally consistent but should be revalidated on the production-shaped implementation before making a final performance claim.

## Proposed implementation

Do **not** upstream the standalone diagnostic graph or add a second graph manager.

Instead, extend the existing MOSS-TTS sampling CUDA Graph from #1303 so the captured graph produces both:

1. `DelaySamplingOutput` / sampled `rows`
2. feedback embeddings derived from those rows via `_prepare_multi_modal_inputs`

Conceptually:

```text
existing sampling CUDA Graph
  -> Delay sampling / FSM
  -> rows
  -> feedback embedding
  -> replay returns rows + feedback embeddings
```

issues.title: [Bug] PD returns empty completions under queue depth; degraded rows share KV slots with live requests
issues.body:
A correctness defect in the PD path, with the measurement that localizes it. It is not a performance issue and it is silent.

## What a user sees

A request returns HTTP 200, `finish_reason: "stop"`, `completion_tokens: 1`, correct `prompt_tokens`, and an empty delta. Two SSE frames, the terminal chunk and `[DONE]`, with no content frame. The single token is 151645, `<|im_end|>`, and it ends the request through `FINISH_MATCHED_TOKEN` as a matched stop token rather than as a member of `eos_token_ids` — so a probe that checks `eos_token_ids` cannot see this population, which cost us one instrumented run.

The response is well formed. Nothing logs an error.

## Rate

PD only. Measured on a clean two-GPU pair with mixed prompt lengths, `mem_fraction_static=0.87`, zero transport errors:

| offered | achieved | in-flight p50 | empty completions per 3000 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | 5.96 | 8 | 0 |
| 8 | 7.92 | 12 | 0 |
| 10 | 9.90 | 20 | 1 |
| 12 | 10.64 | 175 | 24 |
| 16 | 10.91 | 535 | 48 |

A colocated replica under an identical driver produced 0 in 3000, and 0 in 28,472 at the longest prompt length.

## What it is not

**Not the server args PD forces.** A colocated arm with `page_size=1` and `disable_radix_cache` set, same driver, same mixed lengths, same long-lived server, produced zero.

**Not the KV transfer or the handoff.** The single token is sampled by the prefill half before any transfer occurs, so a decode-side probe never fires for this population.

**Not sampling numerics.** Decoding is greedy. Across two runs the failing rows' logit gaps span the control distribution, with a median of 13 bf16 ULP against the control's 9, and four of eleven above 33 ULP. Colocated never places the terminator in its top two: 0 of 2237 prefill rows, against a rate that predicts about 9.8, Poisson p = 5.6e-5.

**Not prefill batch composition.** Raising `prefill_coalesce_requests` from the default to 8 moved mean batch size 2.73 to 3.11 and cut single-request batches from 20.6% to 6.7%, with no rise in the failure rate. Failures occur at batch size 1.

**Not prompt length.** Short prompts fail once queues are deep. An earlier length correlation was queue depth in disguise.

## What it is

The whole logit vector is depressed, not re-ranked. Failing rows sit 7 to 8 logits below control on both the top and second token while the gap between them is preserved. The control distribution does not move at all across the entire rate ladder — median top logit 22.75 at every rate — so depth does nothing to ordinary rows. It creates a distinct population: zero rows below `l1 = 16` across 5989 rows at the two lowest rates, then 1.4%, 3.4% and 6.3% as depth rises.

That shape is a degraded hidden state at the final position, not a ranking or sampling fault.

**Degraded rows share KV slots with a concurrently allocated request. Control rows never do.**

| | degraded (`l1 <= 16`), n=13 | control, n=61 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| shares a slot with a currently-allocated request | 7 (53.8%) | **0 (0.0%)** |
| median / max shared slots | 475 / 7323 | 0 / **0** |
| own mapping internally unique | 13/13 | 61/61 |

Length-controlled: mid-length 4/6 against 0/21, long 3/7 against 0/20. One captured failure had `n=1963` with 1304 of its slots concurrently mapped by another allocated request, its own mapping clean.

Separating "currently allocated" from "recently seen" was what made this readable. Counting both together gives 86.7% against 3.9%, which looks like a rate dif

issues.title: [Feature] Validate Inductor/Triton Compilation for the Fun-ASR Audio Encoder
issues.body:
## Status

Proposed performance and correctness investigation.

Suggested labels: `fun-asr`, `performance`, `torch-compile`, `triton`, `quality`.

## Summary

Fun-ASR already has an opt-in `enable_encoder_torch_compile` path that compiles the SANM audio encoder and multimodal adaptor with dynamic sequence lengths.Encoder-only measurements on an H200 show a substantial steady-state speedup,especially for batched masked inputs. However, the compiled bf16 output is not bitwise identical to eager output, and compiling each input signature has a large cold-start cost.

We should validate end-to-end transcription quality and serving throughput on the full SeedTTS EN and ZH sets before enabling encoder compilation by default.Hand-written Triton kernels should remain out of scope until the existing Inductor path is fully evaluated and a remaining kernel-level bottleneck is demonstrated.

## Motivation

The Fun-ASR audio path contains 70 SANM blocks: 50 encoder blocks and 20 timestamp-prediction blocks. An eager short-audio forward launches hundreds of small normalization, residual, activation, masking, and layout kernels.Inductor can combine many of these operations into generated Triton kernels,reducing launch and memory-traffic overhead without replacing the optimized GEMM, SDPA, or depthwise-convolution implementations.

The optimization is currently disabled by default:

```python
"enable_encoder_torch_compile": False
```

This is the correct default until quality, cold-start behavior, and full serving performance have been measured with real model weights.

## Test Environment

- GPU: NVIDIA H200
- PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130
- Triton: 3.6.0
- dtype: bfloat16
- Model: `FunAudioLLM/Fun-ASR-Nano-2512-hf`
- Model revision: `e296c62e32a328b1d649a8f02701ac54c2fac9f0`

Use a current checkpoint revision. Older revisions used legacy audio parameter names that do not match the current SGLang model implementation.

## Current Measurements

The microbenchmark loaded the real checkpoint weights and ran only the audio encoder and multimodal adaptor. The batched case used right padding and the production SANM mask convention.

| Input | Eager median | Compiled median | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| B=1, T=77, unmasked | 18.95 ms | 13.84 ms | 1.37x |
| B=8, T=77, masked | 28.48 ms | 14.28 ms | 1.99x |

The results confirm a useful steady-state optimization. They do not establish an end-to-end throughput win because preprocessing, scheduling, LLM prefill,and autoregressive decoding are excluded from the microbenchmark.

### Numerical Difference

Eager and compiled outputs were compared in the same process with identical weights and inputs.

| Input | Mean absolute error | Maximum absolute error | Cosine similarity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| B=1, T=77 | 0.183224 | 8.0 | 0.999952376 |
| B=8, T=77 | 0.163603 | 12.0 | 0.999944150 |

These differences are small relative to the output norm but are large enough that encoder tensor closeness alone cannot approve the change. Greedy token generation may amplify a small encoder difference near an LLM decision boundary. Corpus-level transcript and WER comparisons are required.

### Cold Start

Compilation took approximately 42 to 54 seconds for each new input signature during isolated testing. The production warmup covers these signatures:

- B=1 without a mask
- B=1 with a mask
- B>=2 with a mask

The warmup prevents compilation from landing on a user request, but it can add substantial process startup time. The investig

issues.title: [Feature] Add nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b to SGLang-Omni.
issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] This is a feature request rather than a question.
- [x] This issue is written in English.

## Background and Motivation

Add support for [nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b), a 600M-parameter multilingual ASR model based on a 24-layer Cache-Aware FastConformer encoder and an RNN-T decoder.

The model supports 40 language-locales, including 32 locales with out-of-the-box transcription coverage. It provides configurable streaming latency at 80, 160, 320, 560, and 1,120 ms while reusing encoder attention and convolution caches between non-overlapping audio chunks.

| Area | Existing SGLang-Omni ASR paths | Nemotron 3.5 ASR |
|---|---|---|
| Decoder | Mostly Transformer autoregressive decoding | LSTM predictor + RNN-T joint network |
| Streaming state | Primarily request/output streaming | Encoder KV cache, convolution cache, and RNN-T decoder state |
| Language control | Model-specific language hints | Locale prompt or `auto` detection |
| Upstream runtime | Transformers 5.12.1 / SGLang 0.5.16 | Requires Transformers >= 5.13.0 |

Nemotron cannot be treated as another causal language model under the existing RadixAttention decode path. It needs a model-owned RNN-T scheduler and request-scoped streaming state.

## Goals and Scope

### Phase 1: Offline Transcription MVP

- Register `Nemotron3_5AsrForRNNT` with a single `asr` pipeline stage.
- Serve complete audio files through `/v1/audio/transcriptions`.
- Reuse shared mono 16 kHz audio preparation and support batched offline inference.
- Support explicit locales, bare language codes, and `language=auto`.
- Return clean transcripts for `json`/`text` and the detected locale in `verbose_json` when available.

### Phase 2: Native Cache-Aware Streaming

- Add a dedicated scheduler based on `StreamingSimpleScheduler`.
- Preserve encoder attention, convolution, and RNN-T decoder caches per request.
- Process fixed-size chunks for lookahead values `{0, 1, 3, 6, 13}`.
- Batch ready chunks across compatible streams without sharing cache state.
- Add or define an incremental-audio transport; the current `stream=true` response mode must not be described as live audio ingestion.

### Non-goals

GGUF/NeMo-Speech.cpp integration, diarization, word timestamps, fine-tuning, and custom fused RNN-T kernels are outside the initial scope.

## Proposed Design

1. `config.py`: define a single-stage pipeline with architecture `Nemotron3_5AsrForRNNT` and a deployment-level `num_lookahead_tokens` setting, defaulting to `3` (320 ms).
2. `request_builders.py`: prepare 16 kHz audio, validate language prompts, construct processor inputs, and adapt results to `StagePayload`.
3. `scheduler.py`: own request admission, chunk batching, stream lifecycle, cache allocation, abort handling, and final-chunk padding.
4. `model_runner.py`: implement offline batched inference and step-wise RNN-T decoding while carrying encoder and decoder state between chunks.
5. `stages.py`: load `AutoProcessor` and `AutoModelForRNNT` once and expose the scheduler through the normal stage factory.

The Transformers dependency must be resolved explicitly through a coordinated stack upgrade or a narrowly maintained compatibility backport. Installing a second incompatible Transformers version at runtime is not acceptable.

issues.title: [Bug] KV budget uses the global-free-memory fallback in every containerized run, and can over-size the pool
issues.body:
## Summary

`get_process_gpu_memory_bytes` returns 0 in a container, so `_OmniKVCacheConfigurator._profile_available_bytes` never uses NVML accounting and always takes the global free-memory fallback. That fallback races model-load timing, and we measured it size a KV pool ~11.9 GiB too large on a plain colocated single-GPU run.

This is on `main` and is unrelated to prefill/decode work; a PD run happens to make it visible because two halves of one stage size their pools differently.

## Where it breaks

`sglang_omni/utils/gpu_memory.py:125` matches `os.getpid()` against pids from `nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses`. NVML reports pids from the host namespace; the caller runs in a container namespace and sees a different number for itself, so the join never matches and the function returns 0.

NVML itself is fine. In one instrumented worker it reported host pid 546113 holding 59.97 GiB while torch had 59.16 GiB allocated, so the number is both present and accurate. Only the join fails.

`sglang_omni/model_runner/sglang_model_runner.py:87` treats `<= 0` as "NVML unavailable" and falls through to `_profile_available_bytes_from_stage_load_delta`. Every profile line we captured logged `gpu_mem_accounting=stage_load_fallback` with `pre_load_process_mem=0.00GiB`.

Reproducer, inside the container, on any card:

```python
import os, torch, pynvml
buf = torch.empty(int(1e9), dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda:0")
torch.cuda.synchronize()
pynvml.nvmlInit()
h = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)
print(os.getpid(), [p.pid for p in pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetComputeRunningProcesses(h)])
```

The calling pid is absent from the list even though it holds a CUDA context, so the lookup falls through to `return 0`.

## What it costs

`Qwen/Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct`, H200 140.40 GiB, thinker true footprint 57.0-57.6 GiB measured four times.

| Configuration | `stage_load_used` | `available_for_kv` | KV tokens | Card after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| colocated, run A | 45.42 GiB | 76.73 GiB | 838138 | 97.7% |
| colocated, run B | 57.03 GiB | 65.12 GiB | 711261 | 90.9% |

Same script and same config. The fallback is a global free-memory delta, so it undercounts whenever part of the stage's own memory is already resident when the "pre" sample is taken at `scheduling/bootstrap.py:116`. Run A left the card at 97.7%.

The undercount fired in 2 of the runs we did and is not reproducible on demand, so a clean re-run does not refute it.

## A second defect in the same formula

`sglang_omni/utils/gpu_memory.py:223-247` computes `total x fraction - (this stage's own usage)` and never subtracts memory belonging to other tenants. On a card already holding 34 GiB of another process, a stage with `fraction=0.87` budgeted 122.49 GiB and OOMed at launch. This one fails immediately rather than skewing KV quietly, which arguably makes it the more urgent of the two.

## The obvious repair does not work

Mapping the caller to its host pid from inside the container is not possible here. Tested on this cluster:

| Route | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `/proc/self/status` `NSpid` | one value, the container pid; the host pair is visible only when read from the host |
| `/proc/self/sched` | `python3 (363046, ...)`, the container pid |
| host `/proc` mounted into the container | not mounted |
| `/proc/1/status` | `Name: sleep`, so this is a separate pid namespace |

Any fix therefore changes where the number comes from, rather than repairing the lookup. One candidate is `torch.cu

issues.title: [Roadmap] Router & Same-GPU DP
issues.body:
## Goals & context

Serving on H100 is host / CPU-dispatch-bound, not GPU-bound (#907): the GPU sits ~72% idle at single-replica saturation (SM ~28%). Same-GPU DP + CUDA MPS recovers most of that idle (DP3 + MPS = +114% [measured], +134% in db-ol's independent reproduction on #912), but a single-process Python router then becomes the next single-core bottleneck (via-router DP3 lands below via-router DP2, router pinned at 88 to 96% of one core).

The goal is not MPS itself but maximizing single-GPU serving performance, across three layers:

1. **Single-worker efficiency** — cut kernel-launch, sync, Python/GIL, and scheduling overhead (Workstreams 1 & 5 below).
2. **Same-GPU DP × MPS** — when one replica still leaves measurable GPU headroom (recipes section, Workstreams 2 & 3).
3. **Router scaling** — so higher backend capacity doesn't hit a new single-core ceiling (Phases 0–3, Workstream 4).

The serving layer is model-agnostic (Higgs / MOSS / Qwen3-Omni go through the same router path), so the router and DP × MPS tracks cover the MOSS series too; MOSS's intra-worker vocoder bottleneck is orthogonal and stays a separate track.

## Router Phase 0: Streaming relay

Stream proxied responses instead of buffering, removing the byte-growth half of the router cost.
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/920 — merged
- A fix for a pre-existing bug: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/931 — merged
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1014 — overload protection (admission control + unified `--max-connections` semantics), merged
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1071
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1015 — bench-side hardening (keep clients alive on per-request failures), PR open

## Router Phase 1: Python CP/DP router

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1049 — PR open in review
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1077 — process lifecycle: auto-kill orphaned stage workers on parent crash, PR open, approved

Design: one **control-plane** process (registry + health + admin, publishes a routable-worker snapshot) plus **N stateless SO_REUSEPORT relay workers** reading the snapshot. Snapshot IPC measured ~10 us [measured]. Root cause it targets: the single core is ~73% fixed per-request overhead (asyncio + httpx + FastAPI, ~820 qps ceiling even with trivial responses) plus ~27% byte-proportional relay.

- [x] **Real-worker 1-vs-N A/B:** N relay processes lift the single-core ceiling against a real worker pool.
- [x] **Admin routing:** separate CP admin port vs reject-on-DP.
- [x] **LB policy:** `random` / power-of-two (`least_request` is per-process under fan-out).
- [x] **Worker count N:** static vs auto (`cpu_count - k`).
- [ ] **Review (community welcome, = Workstream 4):** process lifecycle, shared state, failure recovery, observability, production-serving behavior.

## Router Phase 2: Rust router

**Owner: @Ratish1.** Target ~1 month per @zhaochenyang20's plan; detailed schedule TBD by owner. (will have separate Roadmap soon)

## Same-GPU DP × MPS recipes
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/986 — guide + KV token cap (merged)
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1037 — equal-KV enforcement (merged; main value: homogeneous, reproducible replicas)
- Benchmark / GPU-idle tooling and reproduction baseline: #912
- Reference guide: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/basic_usage/same_gpu_dp.md

issues.title: [Qwen3-Omni Perf] Code2Wav: wire configurable initial codec chunk size into the Qwen3-Omni vocoder scheduler
issues.body:
## Why

The Qwen3-Omni vocoder scheduler uses one hard-coded chunk size for every chunk, including the first:

- `sglang_omni/models/qwen3_omni/components/code2wav_scheduler.py:60` — `stream_chunk_size: int = 10`, applied uniformly (`:152` accumulate gate feeding `_decode_and_emit`).
- `sglang_omni/models/qwen3_omni/config.py:189` — `factory_args={"device": "cuda"}` only; the factory (`code2wav_scheduler.py:271-289`) already accepts `stream_chunk_size` / `left_context_size` kwargs, but config never passes them.

First-audio latency is bounded below by "wait for a full steady chunk". The shared primitive to fix this already exists — `resolve_initial_codec_chunk_frames` (`sglang_omni/models/tts_streaming.py:11-37`) — and is wired for higgs_tts and moss_tts_local, but `Code2WavScheduler` (a `StreamingSimpleScheduler`) never uses it.

A small first chunk (e.g. 4 frames) with a larger steady chunk (e.g. 25) and 25-frame left context is a sensible starting point, with one seam rule to verify: chunk 1 must use the whole initial chunk as its left context so the overlap-trim stays seamless across the size change. The current clamp `context = min(left_context_size, start)` (`:240`) already gives chunk 1 the full available history, so this is a property to verify with a test, not new logic.

## Scope

1. Make initial and steady chunk sizes configurable for the Qwen3-Omni code2wav stage (config + per-request override via the existing resolve helper).
2. Verify (unit test) the chunk-1 left-context handoff stays seamless across the size change.
3. Fixed-value sweep (initial ∈ {2, 4, 10}, steady ∈ {10, 25}) to pick defaults.

Out of scope: load-adaptive sizing (gated on this sweep, see roadmap), batching (#1026), CUDA graph (#1101). Note steady=25 interacts with #1101's capture shapes — coordinate defaults.

## Approach

1. Thread initial/steady chunk sizes through `config.py` factory_args into `Code2WavScheduler` (the factory kwargs already exist; add the initial size via the shared resolve helper).
2. In the accumulate gate, flush chunk 0 at the initial size; afterwards count from the initial offset.
3. In `_decode_incremental`, verify chunk 1 uses the full initial chunk as left context (current clamp should already do this — lock it with a test).
4. Sweep and record TTFA + steady xRT at c1/c8.

## Quant target + command

TTFA p50 reduction at c1 with no steady-state xRT regression >5%. Speech A/B per the measurement rules in #1018.

## Verification

- Behavior class: generation-changing (chunk boundaries move) — requires the audio-continuity check (no discontinuity at the chunk-0/1 seam) and the declared waveform-boundary gate, not bit-exact audio.
- Unit test: scheduler emits chunk 0 at the initial size, chunk 1 with initial-chunk left context, steady chunks after.

## Deps

None to start. Default choice should land after (or with) #1101 so graph capture shapes match.

Part of #1022. Design and benchmark contract: #1018 (item 4.3).

issues.title: [Bug] Qwen3-TTS same-seed output diverges on first use of an exact prompt at concurrency=1
issues.body:
[Bug/Discussion] Radix cache prefix hit changes FlashInfer FA2 kernel specialization, producing non-deterministic TTS output (cache-invariance gap)

TL;DR

With identical prompt, identical reference wav, identical seed and identical sampling params, Qwen3-TTS on SGLang-Omni produces two different waveforms depending on whether the request hits the radix cache.

The root cause is not KV corruption in the radix cache. The cached prefix KV is bitwise equal to the recomputed prefix KV. The actual chain is:

radix prefix hit
  → q_len changes (58 → 1)
  → FlashInfer FA2 selects a different CTA_TILE_Q specialization
  → different floating-point reduction order
  → ~1 bf16 ULP-scale difference in attention output
  → top-k reordering in the talker logits
  → same seed, same Gumbel draw, same sampled rank, but a different token at that rank
  → autoregressive divergence
  → different wav

I'd like to discuss (a) whether this should be scoped as an SGLang issue, a FlashInfer issue, or an omni-path issue, and (b) which of the candidate fixes below is worth turning into a PR.

Environment

  • SGLang-Omni
  • Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base
  • Single RTX 4090 (SM89), bf16
  • Attention backend: FlashInfer (FA2)

Reproduction

Send the exact same request repeatedly (same text, same reference wav, same seed, same sampling params).

Radix cache ON:

Request 1 → A
Request 2 → B
Request 3 → B
Request 4 → B
Request 5 → B

The ABBBB pattern is stable across repeated rounds. Flushing the cache resets it to A again.

Radix cache OFF:

AAAAA
AAAAA
AAAAA

So the mapping is exactly:

radix MISS → A
radix HIT  → B

This is not jitter — it is fully reproducible and deterministic given the cache state.

What changes between MISS and HIT

  | cached tokens | new tokens | q_len | kv_len -- | -- | -- | -- | -- MISS | 0 | 58 | 58 | 58 HIT | 57 | 1 | 1 | 58

There is a second specialization switch further up (around q_len=33, CTA64 → CTA128), but that one is bitwise identical (A → A). So the claim is not "any kernel switch changes the result" — it is specifically that CTA16 is the divergent tier relative to CTA64/128.

A supplementary sweep on the KV side: kv_len <= 16 gives identical results across shapes, kv_len >= 17 starts to diverge.

3. Different q_len, forced same KernelTraits — the causal experiment

Kept q_len = 1 vs q_len = 58, but forced both to use the same KernelTraits / same CTA_TILE_Q / same specialization, then compared the attention output for the last token:

Attention O → bitwise identical
LSE         → bitwise identical

This nails the causality:

q_len is the dispatch trigger, not the numerical root cause. The numerical difference comes from the different floating-point reduction order between FA2 specializations.

How a ~1 ULP difference becomes a different waveform

Bit-level diff of the last token's attention out

issues.title: MiniMax-Music3 VRAM usage on single-GPU serving much higher than expected
issues.body:
Separately from the dropout bug in [#1542](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/issues/1542), wanted to flag something about VRAM sizing while running MiniMax-Music3 on a single RTX 3090 (24GB).

To get a KV cache pool large enough to avoid the CFG pairing crash ("MiniMax Music 3 decodes conditioned and unconditioned rows as pairs; this batch has 1 rows") on anything beyond very short clips, I had to raise `--mem-fraction-static` well above the default. At 0.75, the computed KV pool was only 7363 tokens, which crashes on most real generations since CFG needs two rows (conditioned + unconditioned) each reserving roughly `prompt_tokens` + `max_frames`. Raising to 0.85 gave a KV pool of 23902 tokens, which reliably covers the model's own documented 5-minute/7500-frame ceiling.

At that 0.85 setting, weights alone load at 16.01GB, and actual generation-time usage sits around 23-24GB out of 24.6GB total, basically the whole card, leaving almost no headroom for anything else running on the same GPU.

Is this expected for the single-GPU serving path? The docs I've seen describe the intended topology as two GPUs (one for LLM generation, one for Flow Matching/waveform decoding), so I'm not sure if the ~23-24GB figure on one card is just what colocating both stages costs, or if there's a config I'm missing that would bring it down. Want to make sure I'm not missing a flag before assuming this is just the real footprint for single-GPU setups.

Happy to share my full compose config / startup logs if useful.

issues.title: [Feature] Idle VRAM release / sleep-wake API for colocated single-GPU deployments
issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

I'm running MiniMax-Music3 alongside a separate LLM inference server (vLLM, which has a built-in Sleep Mode via `/sleep` and `/wake_up` API endpoints) on a single consumer 24GB GPU at home. The two need to take turns using the card, since neither's VRAM footprint fits alongside the other at full size.

sglang-omni/MiniMax-Music3 currently holds its full VRAM footprint (~21.9GB observed) resident for the entire lifetime of the process, whether actively generating or completely idle. There's no idle-timeout unload and no API to explicitly release/reacquire GPU memory on demand, unlike vLLM's Sleep Mode.

My current workaround is external: starting/stopping the whole Docker container around each generation request via the Docker Engine API, so the model's VRAM is only held for the duration of an actual request. This works, but costs a real ~50-58s cold-start penalty on every single generation, since the process (weight load, sglang-omni setup, etc.) restarts from scratch each time.

Would an idle-timeout auto-unload, or an explicit sleep/wake-style API (weights offloaded to host RAM or fully released, then reloadable on demand without a full process restart) be something this project would consider? Even a coarser version than vLLM's (e.g. "unload weights from GPU, keep the process alive") would meaningfully cut that cold-start cost for anyone colocating this on a single card.

Happy to share more details on the exact numbers/setup if useful.

### Related resources

- [#1572](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/issues/1572) - MiniMax-Music3 VRAM usage on single-GPU serving higher than expected (same setup, prior VRAM investigation)
- [#1542](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/issues/1542) - MiniMax-Music3: silent dropout at final-chunk stitching boundary (another issue found while running this same colocated setup)
- [#1605](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/pull/1605) - closed draft PR exploring layerwise-offload for MiniMax-Music3, linked from #1572 - branch was deleted when closed, but the whole-stage CPU/GPU swap approach it prototyped is architecturally close to what an idle-unload mechanism would need

issues.body:
## Goal

This roadmap tracks AutoRound quantization support for SGLang-Omni models on Intel XPU and NVIDIA CUDA backends.

**Please note** that:
This quantization roadmap is downstream of the SGLang-Omni Intel XPU roadmap. We should only claim XPU quantization support after the corresponding XPU backend capability, model coverage, and CI readiness are available and tracked in the XPU roadmap.


The focus is practical community enablement:
- make AutoRound quantized Omni checkpoints easier to load, validate, and benchmark;
- prioritize INT, MXFP4 and MXFP8 schemes quantization support first;
- include native FP8 as a lower-priority follow-up where SGLang backend support already exists or is planned;
- align Omni-side metadata adaptation with actual SGLang backend execution capability;

Omni adapts model/stage metadata, validates contracts, and selects backend policy. SGLang owns the executable quantization path.

issues.title: [RFC][Qwen3-Omni] AutoRound MXFP4/8 Scheme Support
issues.body:
### Motivation

PR #722 added Qwen3-Omni AutoRound INT4 thinker support plus an Omni-side quantization compatibility layer. This RFC extends that support to AutoRound MX exports:

- MXFP4: accepted for Thinker MoE experts only
- MXFP8: W8A8 support for validated Blackwell paths
- Talker/code2wav: remain BF16

The main rule is: Omni may translate AutoRound metadata only for combinations that the pinned SGLang runtime can execute correctly on the target hardware. Unsupported combinations of scheme, layer type, and hardware must fail fast at load time.

Note on MXFP8: MXFP8 is a W8A8 scheme by definition — activations are also
microscaled — so it is **not** a pure metadata-translation problem. The
activation path exercises the MoE kernels, the attention backend, and CUDA Graph
capture. The underlying kernels support this path (native on NVIDIA Blackwell and
on future Intel discrete GPUs based on the Xe3p-XPC architecture, code-named Crescent Island; **CRI** for short,
including the activation-quantization path), but we will still
**validate the activation path in E2E tests before claiming MXFP8 support on the
Omni side.**

### Expected Scope & Support Matrix

MX execution is hardware- and layer-type dependent, so v1 is deliberately narrow
and enforced by the loader.

#### MXFP4 Scope

| Hardware | Thinker MoE experts | Thinker dense/attention | Talker/code2wav | Execution contract |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hopper SM90, H100/H200 | ✅ pending E2E gate | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | SGLang supports MXFP4 MoE through the FlashInfer Cutlass mixed-input path. The AutoRound export is W4A4, but CUDA execution normalizes it to MXFP4 expert weights with BF16 activations (`W4A16`-style execution). The loader must record/log that A4 activations are not preserved. |
| Blackwell SM100, B200/GB200 | ✅ pending E2E gate | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | SGLang `flashinfer_mxfp4_moe_precision=default` quantizes activations with `mxfp8_quantize` (`W4A8`-style execution), while `flashinfer_mxfp4_moe_precision=bf16` keeps BF16 activations (`W4A16`-style execution). There is no A4 activation-preserving CUDA path. The loader must record/log that A4 activations are not preserved. |
| Blackwell SM120 | 🟡 pending validation | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | This path should be treated as `W4A8`-style execution, not `W4A16`, and not as preserved AutoRound W4A4. It requires separate SM120 E2E validation. |
| Intel XPU CRI | 🟡 future work | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | No SGLang main-source or merged-PR evidence exists for an Intel XPU W4A4 MXFP4 backend yet. The [Intel XPU roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/24922) lists MXFP as future functional support. |
| Other NVIDIA | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | No plan. |

#### MXFP8 Scope

MXFP8 is W8A8: weights and activations are microscaled. It is not only metadata translation. It touches dense kernels, MoE kernels, activation quantization, and CUDA Graph capture.

There is no Hopper dequant-to-BF16 MXFP8 fallback in the current/pinned SGLang path. Hopper MXFP8 must be rejected unless new SGLang-side fallback work is added explicitly.

| Hardware | Thinker MoE experts | Thinker dense/attention | Talker/code2wav | Execution contract |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hopper SM90, H100/H200 | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | ❌ rejected | Current SGLang MXFP8 MoE requires SM100 on CUDA, and dense MXFP8 requires Blackwell-class CUDA paths. |
| Blackwell SM100, B200/GB200 | ✅ pending E2E gate | ✅ pending E2E gate

issues.title: [Bug] MiniMax-Music3: silent dropout at final-chunk stitching boundary
issues.body:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version.
- [x] 3. Please note that if the bug-related issue you submitted lacks corresponding environment info and a minimal reproducible demo, it will be challenging for us to reproduce and resolve the issue, reducing the likelihood of receiving feedback.
- [x] 4. If the issue you raised is not a bug but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 5. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Generating audio with MiniMax-Music3 via `sgl-omni serve`, I'm seeing a reproducible near-total silent gap in the output audio, occurring specifically at the handoff into the final acoustic chunk.

Measured directly on the output WAV (RMS amplitude in 0.25s windows): amplitude drops to noise-floor level (~74–79 out of 0–32767) from 11.25s to 13.75s, a clean 2.5-second silent gap, then jumps immediately back to full amplitude (~7400+) at 14.00s. Real audio exists both before and after the gap.

Server log shows the dropout timing correlates directly with the chunk-stitching boundary: chunk 1 covers 4.0–12.0s and the final chunk (idx=2, `final=True`) covers 8.0–16.0s, with their overlap region at 8.0–12.0s. The dropout sits right at the tail of that overlap and bleeds into the final chunk's exclusive range, pointing at the crossfade/stitching logic specifically when handling the transition into the final chunk.

### Reproduction

Request:

`max_new_tokens: 400` (16s of audio)
Prompt: simple, unstructured (`"Generate an 8 bar loop. make it funky"`)
`finish_reason=length` (completed normally, not an early stop)

Server log, acoustic chunks:

```
idx=0 frames=200 frame_range=[0,200) final=False
idx=1 frames=200 frame_range=[100,300) final=False
idx=2 frames=200 frame_range=[200,400) final=True
```

Single GPU: RTX 3090 (24GB)
`--mem-fraction-static 0.85`

issues.title: [CI] Add durable, non-gating CI observability
issues.body:
## Goal

Add persistent observability for Omni CI without changing CI behavior.

Observability must not affect:
- exit codes or retry behavior
- thresholds or test selection
- CPU/GPU scheduling
- runner behavior

Observability failures must never fail CI.

## Plan

### PR A — Durable CI observations

Persist versioned, immutable observation records under:

```text
<ci-data-dir>/observations/
```

Collect existing signals only:

* run / job / stage / commit metadata
* per-attempt timestamps and exit codes from <test-wrapper-script>
* existing benchmark result JSON
* existing CPU contention statistics
* basic environment metadata

Requirements:

* include `schema_version`
* use one file per stage attempt; no shared concurrent JSONL append
* emit each attempt when it completes
* use an `EXIT` trap for wrapper-level terminal-path coverage
* all telemetry writes are best-effort and preserve the original exit code
* observability added to `omni-post-stage` must run after GPU cleanup
* add bounded retention / GC for observation records
* keep `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` concise; exclude `per_sample` / `per_request`

### PR B — Reconcile missing observations

In-job telemetry cannot cover every interrupted job. Use the GitHub Actions jobs API as the source of truth for job lifecycle and join local observations as enrichment.

Record jobs with missing or partial telemetry instead of silently excluding them.

Start with two reports:

* First-attempt pass rate by stage
* Retry wall time by stage

## Non-goals

Not part of this issue:

* retry or verdict changes
* resource-validity gating
* CPU isolation changes
* automatic performance regression detection
* performance comparability policy
* alerting
* Prometheus / Grafana / ClickHouse

Existing throughput, latency, RTF, and quality results should be preserved, but interpreting their trends is separate work.

## Acceptance criteria

* CI behavior is unchanged whether observability succeeds or fails.
* Observation history survives PR/run cleanup.
* Concurrent jobs cannot corrupt each other's records.
* Attempt history and retry time are recoverable.
* Cancelled, timed-out, or otherwise incomplete jobs are not silently omitted.
* First-attempt pass rate and retry wall time can be queried by stage.

issues.title: [RFC] Unify configuration interfaces and resolution
issues.body:
## Motivation

SGLang-Omni currently accepts configuration through model Python defaults, Pipeline YAML, dynamic dotted CLI options, dedicated typed CLI options, environment variables, and Router launcher YAML.

Multiple inputs are useful, but the same setting can follow different code paths for path resolution, type conversion, precedence, validation, and mutation. This creates three usability and maintenance problems:

1. Adding one setting can require duplicate YAML and CLI validation/mutation logic.
2. Developers do not have a single rule for deciding whether a setting belongs in the typed schema, CLI, `factory_args`, `runtime_overrides`, or a model-specific config.
3. Users do not have a clear way to discover where to change a setting or explain which source produced the final value.

## Proposal documents

- [Configuration Interface Refactoring Design Proposal (English)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/sunao/config-interface-refactor-proposal/docs/design/configuration_interface_refactor_proposal_en.md)
- [配置接口重构设计 Proposal（中文）](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/sunao/config-interface-refactor-proposal/docs/design/configuration_interface_refactor_proposal.md)

Notion mirror: https://www.notion.so/maydomain/Configuration-Refactor-Proposal-for-sglang-omni-3b84e1dff05a808a8076ea49cf9a9a7e

## Proposed direction

Introduce one canonical typed configuration schema and one resolver:

- YAML remains a model-template overlay for persistent, reviewable Pipeline configuration.
- CLI keeps service-process options and uses `--set PATH=VALUE` for temporary Pipeline overrides.
- YAML, CLI, compatibility aliases, and Router worker settings all produce the same source-aware `ConfigPatch` representation.
- A single `ConfigResolver` owns type conversion, precedence, conflict detection, validation, and provenance.
- Runtime planners consume an immutable resolved config; derived runtime values remain outside the user configuration.
- Router launcher YAML replaces `worker_extra_args` shell fragments with structured worker config and `set` values.

Related historical issue: #107. That issue addressed earlier field-placement problems; this RFC covers the broader interface and resolution model.

## Tracking milestones

- [ ] Agree on ownership boundaries and the canonical path model
- [ ] Add `ConfigPatch`, source provenance, and a unified resolver without changing current resolved behavior
- [ ] Add `config schema`, `validate`, `resolve`, `explain`, and `migrate` commands
- [ ] Introduce opt-in schema v2 with model-template overlays, name-keyed stages, and YAML `set:`
- [ ] Convert dedicated runtime CLI options into compatibility aliases that only emit patches
- [ ] Replace Router `worker_extra_args` with structured worker configuration
- [ ] Migrate official examples and documentation
- [ ] Deprecate and remove overlapping v1 configuration paths according to the compatibility plan

## Success criteria

- A public setting is defined and validated once.
- YAML and CLI forms for the same path resolve to the same value.
- Developers have an explicit decision table for adding public, model-specific, service, request-time, and derived settings.
- Users can discover valid paths and inspect the final value and its source before startup.

issues.title: [Whisper] Concurrent serving crashes: asr scheduler AssertionError, then connection refused
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

Whisper serving crashes under concurrent load: the asr scheduler thread dies with `AssertionError: Expected 8, got -404`, after which every request gets connection refused. A single request works; closed-loop c8, c16, and c32 all kill the server within seconds.

```
[ERROR] sglang_omni.pipeline.stage.runtime: Scheduler thread for stage asr crashed
AssertionError: Expected 8, got -404
[ERROR] sglang_omni.serve.transcriptions: Error transcribing audio for request ...
RuntimeError: scheduler crashed: Expected 8, got -404
```

## Reproduction

```
sgl-omni serve --model-path openai/whisper-large-v3 --port 8103
# then closed loop, concurrency 8, POST /v1/audio/transcriptions
# with tests/data/query_to_cars.wav (5 s); server dies within seconds
```

1x H200, sglang 0.5.16, head 29f16e8b. Found while running the multi-model campaign for #1463 with the CPU allocator off, so it is unrelated to that change; it kept Whisper out of that PR's benchmark table.

issues.title: [Qwen3-Omni Perf] Code2Wav: CUDA-graph shape hit-rate telemetry
issues.body:
## Why

PR #1101 (open) adds exact-shape CUDA-graph replay for code2wav, enabled by default (+7.8% req/s @c8 on H100). Its benefit depends entirely on incoming shapes hitting captured buckets — capture is limited to `B1/T{10,20,30,35}` — so a shape drift (different chunk sizes after the initial-chunk work, ragged batches from #1026) degrades to eager.

#1101 already counts fallbacks per reason (`disabled`/`ineligible`/`key_miss`) and replays in aggregate, but logs them only once at scheduler startup, before real traffic. What is missing: per-shape granularity and periodic/shutdown reporting, so operators can verify hit rate under real traffic and tune capture buckets from data instead of guesses.

## Scope

Env-gated (e.g. `SGLANG_OMNI_TRACE_CODE2WAV_GRAPH=1`, matching the `SGLANG_OMNI_TRACE_*` precedent) extension of #1101's existing counters: per-shape hit count, per-shape eager-fallback count, periodic log line (or dump at shutdown). No behavior change when disabled.

## Approach

1. Extend #1101's `_fallback_counts` / replay counters to key on shape (`Counter[(shape_key)]`) for hit vs fallback.
2. Log a summary every N decodes or on stage shutdown.
3. Zero overhead when the env var is unset (single `if` on a cached bool).

## Quant target + command

None (observability). Acceptance: stats output matches a constructed workload with known hit/miss mix.

## Verification

- Behavior class: behavior-preserving (no numeric change; disabled by default).
- Unit test with a fake shape sequence asserting counter contents.

## Deps

PR #1101 must land first (builds on its graph path and counters). Pairs naturally with the initial-chunk sizing issue — the sweep there should be run with stats on.

Part of #1022. Design and benchmark contract: #1018 (item 4.6).

issues.title: [Qwen3-Omni Perf] Encoder batch-wait sweep: tune hard-coded max_batch_wait_ms
issues.body:
## Why

Both encoder stage factories hard-code the batching wait window:

- `sglang_omni/models/qwen3_omni/stages.py:852` (image encoder factory) and `stages.py:922` (audio encoder factory), both `max_batch_wait_ms=50`; `factory_args` in `config.py:56-70` passes only `{device, dtype}`, so there is no override.

Every multimodal request waits up to 50 ms inside the encoder stage just to form a batch, before any compute starts — including a lone request: `SimpleScheduler._collect_batch` (`sglang_omni/scheduling/simple_scheduler.py:101-130`) blocks the full window on an empty queue, with no fast path. That sits directly on the TTFT/TTFA critical path. The 50 was chosen so c16 video benchmarks batch together (comment at `stages.py:846`), but it has never been swept; low-concurrency traffic almost certainly wants a smaller window.

## Scope

1. Expose `max_batch_wait_ms` as a config value with the current 50 as default (no behavior change by default).
2. Sweep {0, 1, 5, 10, 50} under the standard multimodal workload at c1/c8/c16.
3. Propose the TTFT/TTFA-optimal value as the new default, keeping the override.

Out of scope: encoder batching policy changes beyond the wait window; encoder caching (measured-negative, see roadmap).

## Approach

1. Thread the value from stage config → encoder factory args (mirror how other stage knobs are plumbed in `config.py` / `stages.py`).
2. Run the mm benchmark (`benchmarks/tasks/audio_understanding.py` or `benchmarks/eval/benchmark_omni_mmmu.py --enable-audio`) once per value per concurrency; three repeats at the decision points.
3. Report TTFT p50/p95 and TTFA p50 per value; pick the knee.

## Quant target + command

TTFT/TTFA improvement at c1 with no regression at c16. This is a measurement-first task — a "50 is already optimal" result is a valid, landable outcome (config exposure still ships).

## Verification

- Behavior class: behavior-preserving at default (50 stays default until the sweep justifies a change); outputs identical.
- Unit test: factory receives the configured value; default unchanged.

## Deps

None. Good entry task: touches config plumbing + benchmark harness only, no concurrency or CUDA lifetime risk.

Part of #1022. Design and benchmark contract: #1018 (item 2.7).

issues.title: Stage 11 (Video-AMME Talker, FP8 Thinker TP=2) — Performance Investigation
issues.body:
### Goal
Stage 11 (Video-AMME Talker, FP8 Thinker TP=2) latency was ~148–170 s; a GPU snapshot (GPU0 100% / GPU1 4%) suggested load-imbalance and TP-ing code2wav was considered. This issue tracked the full investigation. **Resolved** — see TL;DR.

---

## TL;DR (final, supersedes the original per-phase reading below)
- **Root cause was NOT the talker AR decode** — it was **delivery-bound**. The thinker sat idle ~130 s with a full queue while `mm_aggregate` did a full materialize + re-serialize of the ~55 MiB video embeds under concurrency-16 head-of-line pressure on the relay. Every compute stage is small (~30 s total); both GPUs were ~85 % idle. The original "talker_ar 164 s dominant" number was stage **wall-lifetime (idle-spinning)**, not busy time — corrected in Updates 7–8.
- **Fix: #808 lazy `TensorRef`** (publish embeds to the relay once, forward a ref, resolve once): **165 s → 33 s (~5×)**, accuracy preserved (reproduced in Update 9). Equivalent to the pre-#808 **payload reduction #804** — both attack the same stall.
- **After #808 the latency floor (~30 s) is the talker AR decode = audio length** (`corr(audio_duration, latency)=0.96` vs `corr(prompt_tokens, latency)=0.49`). The only same-architecture lever below ~30 s is shortening the generated audio/answer length (eval-config, bounded by the accuracy 0.40 / WER 0.0175 gates).
- **Low GPU util (70–90 % idle) is the expected signature of a latency-bound benchmark at low concurrency (10 reqs / 4 unique videos), not a balance bug.**

## Levers evaluated — all exhausted, redundant, or blocked
| Lever | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Vision-encoder data-parallel | bit-exact but encode is 0.19 s → wrong target; reverted |
| Parallelize CPU preprocessing | preprocessing 0.79 s/req → non-bottleneck |
| Talker TP=2 | **blocked**: FP8 MoE intermediate 384 → 192/rank, not divisible by quant `block_n=128` |
| Talker cuda-graph | no latency win + #408 RNG-under-graph correctness risk (~5% garbage audio) |
| Talker async one-step lookahead | **slower** (host-bound, `event.query hit=1600 miss=0`) |
| Talker K-frame multi-step decode | no effect (K=1 30.1 s vs K=4 31.2 s) |
| GPU rebalance (code2wav→GPU0, thinker mem 0.40→0.50) | clean / no OOM / PASSES, but latency & util unchanged at this concurrency |
| Payload reduction (frames 128→64) **on top of #808** | prompt tokens halved, but **redundant** → no latency change (the stall #808 already removed) |

**Reusable side result:** with code2wav on GPU0, the thinker mem-fraction safely rises to **0.50** (the `0.40` from #765 was an over-conservative OOM workaround) — headroom for a higher-concurrency *throughput* config, not for this latency metric.

**Bottom line:** #808 (and/or #804) is the win; remaining headroom is audio/answer length, not infra, placement, or talker kernels. Detailed methodology + data in the comments (Updates 7→8→9→10→11 + consolidated Summary).

---
